claims.text: What the image looks like Apical fibronodular opacities, upper-lobe cavitation → reactivation tuberculosis
claims.quote: Apical fibronodular opacities, upper-lobe cavitation Reactivation tuberculosis

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) In adults, a multinodular infiltrate above or behind the clavicle is most characteristic of active TB and suggests reactivation; best seen on an apical-lordotic view or chest CT
claims.quote: In adults, a multinodular infiltrate above or behind the clavicle is most characteristic of active TB; it suggests reactivation of disease. It is best visualized in an apical-lordotic view (a view designed to improve the visualization of the lung apices by elevating the clavicles) or on a chest CT scan.

claims.text: Example: a right upper lobe cavitary lesion on CXR
claims.quote: This image shows a right upper lobe cavitary lesion (arrows) on a chest radiograph of a patient with tuberculosis.

claims.text: Why the apices: reactivation occurs most often there, presumably because of high oxygen tension, lower blood perfusion and reduced immune surveillance
claims.quote: reactivation occurs most often in the lung apices, presumably because of high oxygen tension, lower blood perfusion, and reduced immune surveillance.

claims.text: Causes Infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis: an asymptomatic latent period often follows the first infection, and in a proportion of people it reactivates to active disease
claims.quote: Tuberculosis (TB) is infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis; initial infection is often followed by an asymptomatic latent period, which in a proportion of people reactivates to symptomatic active TB disease.

claims.text: Spread almost exclusively by inhaling airborne droplet nuclei
claims.quote: TB is transmitted almost exclusively through inhalation of airborne particles (droplet nuclei) containing M. tuberculosis.

claims.text: Active disease is much more likely with impaired immunity, particularly HIV infection
claims.quote: Active disease is much more likely in patients with impaired immunity, particularly those with HIV infection.

claims.text: Symptoms Chronic cough is the most common symptom
Low-grade fever is common but not universally present; drenching night sweats are a classic symptom but not specific for TB
claims.quote: Low-grade fever is common but not universally present. Drenching night sweats are a classic symptom but are not specific for TB.

claims.text: High suspicion with fever, cough > 2 to 3 weeks, hemoptysis, night sweats, weight loss and/or lymphadenopathy, or a suspected exposure
claims.quote: The clinical suspicion for pulmonary TB is high in patients who have fever, cough lasting > 2 to 3 weeks, hemoptysis, night sweats, weight loss, and/or lymphadenopathy and in patients with suspected TB exposure

claims.text: Treatment and next step Her chart: airborne isolation; RIPE therapy
Confirm by sputum testing (molecular testing, microscopy and culture)
claims.quote: confirm by sputum testing (molecular testing, microscopic examination, and culture).

claims.text: The four first-line drugs — isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide and ethambutol — are generally given together as initial treatment of active TB
claims.quote: The 4 first-line medications isoniazid (INH), rifampin (RIF) (rifampicin), pyrazinamide (PZA), and ethambutol (EMB) are generally given in combination as initial treatment of active TB.

claims.text: Pyrazinamide in the intensive first 2 months shortens total therapy to 6 months
claims.quote: When used during the intensive initial 2 months of TB treatment, it shortens the total duration of therapy to 6 months and prevents development of resistance to RIF.

claims.text: Ethambutol: main potential toxicity is optic neuritis — the first symptom is inability to tell blue from green
claims.quote: Its main potential toxicity is optic neuritis, which is more common at higher doses (eg, 25 mg/kg) and in patients with impaired renal function. Initial symptoms of optic neuritis are an inability to distinguish blue from green;
